title: Bee nutrition through the seasons
subtitle: What honeybee colonies need to eat, and when, across the UK bee year.
excerpt: A colony's nutritional needs change entirely from January to December. Protein from pollen drives brood rearing in spring and summer; carbohydrates from nectar and honey fuel winter clustering and spring build-up. Understanding what the colony needs in each season, and what the landscape is or is not providing, is the basis for every good supplemental feeding decision.

content.text: Honeybees need two main food sources: nectar and honey for energy (carbohydrate), and pollen for protein, fats, vitamins, and minerals. The balance between them determines whether a colony builds up well in spring, works a summer flow, and survives winter.
Winter: living on stores
Through the winter months the colony lives in a
cluster

and consumes stored honey for energy. A standard National hive colony needs roughly 15 to 20 kg of stores to survive a UK winter. There is no pollen coming in after October in most locations, and no brood rearing (or very little) before late January in a cold season. The colony is at its lowest nutritional demand: it simply needs enough honey to keep warm and alive.

A winter colony that is light on stores requires fondant or candy board feeding, not syrup. Syrup cannot be evaporated to honey in cold weather: it remains wet and ferments. Fondant is dry enough to feed without humidity risk.
Late winter to spring: the protein hunger gap
From late January onward the queen begins laying in a widening brood nest, even in cold weather. This creates a protein demand: young nurse bees need pollen to develop their
hypopharyngeal glands

and produce royal jelly for larvae. The first pollen comes from snowdrops, hazel, and willow catkins, often from mid-February in southern England. In a cold spring or a northern location, the pollen gap can stretch to late March.

A colony that runs out of stored pollen before fresh pollen arrives will stall its brood-rearing, producing fewer bees for the spring build-up. Protein supplements (pollen substitute patties or dried pollen from a previous season) can bridge this gap.
Spring and early summer: the build-up

From March to June, with rising pollen from fruit blossom, dandelion, field beans, and early summer flowers, a healthy colony rears bees rapidly. This is the period of highest nutritional demand: large brood areas require sustained pollen intake. A strong
nectar flow
from oil seed rape, hawthorn, and fruit crops also provides the carbohydrate needed to feed the expanding population.

Beekeepers rarely need to supplement during a good spring. The role at this stage is to ensure the colony has enough space (brood boxes, supers) to store incoming food and expand the brood nest without triggering swarm congestion.
Summer: the flow or the dearth

In the UK, the main summer flow usually runs from June into July depending on the local forage. Clover, lime, borage, and phacelia are the key summer sources. After the flow ends in late July, many locations enter a dearth with little nectar or pollen available until ivy flowers in September. A large colony emerging from the summer flow may consume its stores faster than it can replenish them in a dearth: this is the period when robbing and starvation risk are both highest.
Autumn: ivy and the last stores

Ivy flowers from late September and provides both nectar and pollen in quantity. Ivy honey is excellent winter stores: it sets hard in the comb, does not ferment, and provides energy through the cluster period. A colony that works ivy well will often top up to adequate winter stores without supplemental feeding. However, ivy nectar also contains aromatic compounds that set rapidly in the comb, which can trap bees if a very cold snap follows the ivy flow.
Supplemental feeding: when it helps
Late winter or early spring: pollen supplement patties when no natural pollen is coming in and brood rearing has started.
Early spring: 1:1 sugar syrup to stimulate build-up when stores are low and temperatures are above 12 degrees.
Autumn: 2:1 sugar syrup in September to top up stores before the cluster forms. Aim for the colony to have 15 to 20 kg of sealed stores before October.
Winter: fondant or candy board if the colony is found to be light on stores during a mid-winter heft check.

The quality of local forage varies enormously. An urban or suburban apiary surrounded by allotments, gardens, and parks often has better year-round nutrition than a rural apiary in intensive arable farmland where monocultures provide a brief intense flow followed by nutritional desert.
